title: Can Deterministic Network Verification Reduce Undetected Faults in LLM‑Generated Configurations?
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study id c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) to measure whether inserting a deterministic network verifier between an LLM intent→configuration generator and an emulated execution reduces the proportion of configurations that would execute with operational faults. Using shared_initial_candidate semantics (one identical LLM candidate per intent evaluated both without and with verification), we evaluated 72 preregistered paired intents with gpt-5-mini and a canonical deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed with 144 episodes (72 pairs) and 72 model calls. All baseline executions produced no emulator-observed faults (n_11 = 72, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0). The paired difference in undetected‑fault proportion is 0.0 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate contract this degenerate confirmatory outcome is expected when identical generated candidates produce no baseline execution faults. We report the preregistration rationale, deterministic execution accounting, representative validator diagnostics, exact inferential outputs, and artifact‑grounded recommendations for follow‑on confirmatory designs able to detect verifier utility under realistic baseline‑error regimes.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate high‑level operator intents into device‑level network configurations. This intent→configuration automation can speed change pipelines but risks silently violating reachability, access‑control, ordering, or workflow invariants and thereby causing outages if generated text is executed without additional checks. A standard operational mitigation is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) architecture that combines stochastic LLM generation with deterministic verification and, if needed, repair or human review. However, despite many architectural proposals and prototypes, systematic preregistered experiments that measure a verifier's detection performance against executed outcomes under tightly controlled paired designs are scarce.

This paper answers a narrowly scoped, preregistered research question: does inserting a deterministic network verifier between an LLM generator and emulator execution materially reduce the proportion of configurations that execute with operational faults when the identical generated candidate is evaluated both without and with verification? That estimand isolates verifier detection from improvements that could arise from re‑sampling, prompt‑engineering, or repair‑enabled iterations. We executed study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001 using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 across 72 preregistered paired intents under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The run completed with no technical failures, produced a degenerate confirmatory outcome (no baseline emulator faults), and yields a paired difference of 0.0 (95% CI [0.0,0.0], exact McNemar p = 1.0). Rather than treating this as a null failure, we analyze why it occurred given the preregistered contract and archived artifacts, and we provide concrete, artifact‑grounded guidance for designs that can detect verifier utility when baseline error prevalence is non‑negligible.
sections.related_work:
Work on LLM‑driven NetOps spans intent→configuration translation, multi‑agent/tool‑augmented orchestration, and architectural proposals for combining stochastic generation with deterministic checks. Prior empirical studies demonstrate that modern LLMs can produce device‑level configurations from high‑level intent in constrained vendor‑dialect settings and curated evaluation suites; these results show promise but are typically scoped to limited task families and curated datasets rather than broad production traces [1]. That line of work motivates leveraging LLMs to reduce operator effort while highlighting the need for safety controls when configuration semantics and ordering matter.

Complementing single‑agent generation work, multi‑agent and tool‑augmented frameworks have been proposed that explicitly integrate verifiers, tool calls, or specialized modules into LLM‑driven NetOps pipelines to reduce regressions and coordinate multi‑step changes [2]. These systems illustrate practical architectures for inserting deterministic checks or domain services into agentic workflows, and their evaluations commonly rely on emulators, curated scenarios, or prototype deployments. Such prototypes suggest feasible integration points for verifiers but do not, in the supplied records, provide preregistered paired measurements of verifier detection performance against executed faults.

A related strand of work articulates and evaluates GVR patterns outside NetOps—particularly in code and software repair—where stochastic generators produce candidates that deterministic checkers validate and, when necessary, trigger repair iterations [3]. Those studies document how deterministic validation can convert nondeterministic generation into a correctness‑convergent workflow; they also show that empirical utility depends strongly on baseline generator error rates and on whether the architecture permits verifier‑triggered repairs or resampling. Canonical deterministic network‑verification techniques (e.g., header‑space style analyzers) provide precise invariants for reachability and ACL‑style checks and are natural candidates for the verify stage [4]. The supplied literature therefore motivates a preregistered, paired measurement that isolates verifier detection on identical candidates; our study targets that gap.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001 and froze the confirmatory design before observing final outcomes. The primary estimand is the paired reduction in undetected operational‑fault proportion (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). H1 targeted an absolute paired reduction of 0.20 (two‑sided α = 0.05, power ≥ 0.80); a sample‑size heuristic yielded ≈63 pairs and we preregistered N = 72 pairs stratified equally across three task‑difficulty strata.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and experimental contract. The execution contract enforced shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent we requested exactly one initial LLM generation and evaluated that identical candidate in two paired conditions. Baseline: execute the shared candidate in an isolated emulator and record whether emulator‑observed operational faults occur. Guarded: run the canonical deterministic verifier on the same candidate; if the verifier flags violations the guarded outcome is recorded as prevented (no executed fault); if the verifier does not flag, execute the identical candidate in the emulator and record the result. Under these semantics any observed paired difference can only arise from the verifier preventing the execution of a candidate that would otherwise have failed at emulation.

Model, adapter, and verifier configuration (archival grounding). The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini, requested via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; the canonical verifier was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 configured to apply a full intent‑constraint validation rule set. The archived model configuration record documents declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini", provider = "openai_responses", max_output_tokens = 2000, and maximum_attempts_per_call = 1. The archived verifier traces include structured fields (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration, validation_before/after snapshots, violation_codes, and violation_count) that mechanistically determine guarded decisions. (For clarity: the archived model configuration records temperature = null; null indicates provider‑default sampling semantics rather than an explicit numeric temperature setting.)

Task bank, contamination checks, and stratification. Confirmatory tasks were deterministically generated by a task generator that encodes each intent as: a natural‑language description, an ordered required_sequence of device‑field changes, allowed_touched_fields, initial/expected_final_state snapshots, and a difficulty.level tag (medium/hard/very_hard). The preregistration specified exact‑match contamination checks against public corpora and an exclusion rule for exact matches; no confirmatory pairs were excluded. The confirmatory sample used 24 pairs per difficulty stratum as preregistered.

Execution protocol, retries, and accounting. The missingness plan allowed up to two retries for transient hosted‑API errors; provider calls, retries, and timestamps were logged in the archived execution manifest. The run attempted the preregistered episodes, completed all planned episodes, recorded one shared generation per pair, and produced a complete execution manifest and analysis bundle archived with the study. Per‑episode verifier traces and emulator results were recorded for audit.

Scoring and analysis. Episodes were scored by the verifier's full_intent_constraint_validation rule set. The primary analysis used a paired binary analysis executor (a McNemar‑style exact test where discordant pairs exist) and computed paired bootstrap‑percentile 95% CIs (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729). Pre‑specified subgroup confirmatory tests used Holm correction; pre‑registered sensitivity analyses included treating excluded pairs conservatively as failures and bootstrap diagnostics for detector detection and false‑positive rates. All analysis was executed by deterministic scripts and archived.
sections.results:
Execution and manifest summary. The autonomous pipeline completed without technical failures. Key run figures (archived): planned_episode_count = 144; completed_episode_count = 144; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 72; artifact_count = 510. The archived condition summary reports baseline successes = 72, baseline failures = 0 (success_rate = 1.0) and guarded successes = 72, guarded failures = 0 (success_rate = 1.0).

Paired contingency and inferential outputs. Aggregating across the 72 confirmatory pairs produced contingency counts n_11 = 72, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0 (guarded × baseline). The paired estimate paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples) is [0.0, 0.0]. These tabulations and the archived contingency artifact ground the numerical conclusion.

Representative validator diagnostics. Representative per‑episode traces archived for audit illustrate why no flags occurred on the shared candidates. Examples (excerpted):
- pair‑000001 (difficulty = medium): parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, violation_count = 0.
- pair‑000002 (difficulty = hard): parsed_command_count = 2, required_command_count = 2, violation_count = 0.
- pair‑000003 (difficulty = hard): parsed_command_count = 6, required_command_count = 6, violation_count = 0.
Across representative episodes the verifier parsed the generated sequences, found required commands present in order, and emitted zero violations; no automated repair was applied.

Contamination, missingness, and sensitivity diagnostics. Exact‑match contamination checks flagged zero confirmatory items and no confirmatory episode was excluded or failed; archived missingness summaries confirm complete_pair_count = 72. The preregistered sensitivity analyses were executed and reproduce the degenerate numeric conclusion because no pairs were excluded and no discordant outcomes occurred.
sections.discussion:
Confirmatory interpretation. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the paired estimand measures only verifier detection on identical candidates. When identical generated candidates produce zero emulator faults the paired difference necessarily equals zero; the algebraic ceiling is therefore an expected, reproducible outcome of the design and observed data (n_11 = 72; paired difference = 0.0; McNemar p = 1.0).

Artifact‑grounded diagnostic factors. The archived artifacts permit concrete attribution of this ceiling outcome to measurable pipeline factors. First, the task generator produced intents with explicit sequencing and allowed‑field constraints that reduce ambiguity and raise the probability of a correct single‑shot generation. Second, the declared model repeatedly produced sequences that matched these structured constraints. Third, the verifier's rule set enforces the same intent constraints encoded in the task manifests; per‑episode traces show parsed_command_count = required_command_count and violation_count = 0 for representative tasks. These aligned choices—constrained intents, congruent verifier rules, and model outputs that matched required sequences—explain the absence of baseline emulator faults.

Design and statistical implications. A paired confirmatory test targeting an absolute reduction requires a non‑zero baseline prevalence of executed faults to have power. When baseline prevalence is zero the paired difference must be zero regardless of verifier sensitivity. This algebraic consequence implies that confirmatory designs intended to measure verifier detection should ensure the task bank yields measurable baseline errors (for example, by including ambiguous intents, adversarial cases, or known failure‑mode seeds) or should permit architecture changes (resampling, repair) that allow the verifier to alter the executed candidate distribution.

Concrete preregisterable alternatives to detect verifier utility. The archived pipeline supports several preregisterable modifications that would produce non‑degenerate inferential opportunity without inventing new artifacts: (1) independent‑generation arms—request separate initial generation calls per condition so the guarded arm can benefit from different samples; (2) repair‑enabled flows—allow verifier‑triggered deterministic repair or a single automated repair call and then execute the repaired candidate to measure prevented faults; (3) adversarial/fault‑injection task banks—include intent instances known to elicit generator failures to raise baseline error prevalence; (4) sampling‑parameter sweeps and multi‑model comparisons—explicitly set sampling parameters (non‑null temperature) and test multiple model versions; and (5) explicit false‑positive cost arms—measure blocking costs where verifier flags are treated as operational interventions. Each alternative is preregisterable and implementable with the same deterministic accounting used here; the archived manifests and analysis scripts provide a reproducible template for these follow‑on designs.

Threats to validity revisited. Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics isolates detector performance but prevents verifier‑mediated resampling or repair effects; provider‑call audit confirms one shared generation per pair. Construct validity: emulator‑observed faults are a surrogate for operational harm but do not capture traffic‑dependent timing or vendor‑hardware idiosyncrasies. External validity: experiments used one declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and a synthetic task bank; extrapolation to different models, broader real‑world distributions, or production hardware is limited. Conclusion validity: with zero baseline faults the preregistered power analysis (targeting a 0.20 absolute reduction) is moot; future confirmatory designs must align expected baseline prevalence with power targets.

Operational implications. The observed ceiling does not imply verifiers are unnecessary in practice. Rather, it shows that under constrained, high‑clarity intents and a verifier rule set that encodes the same constraints an LLM can produce device‑level sequences that pass deterministic checks and emulator execution. Measuring the verifier's net operational value requires explicit, preregistered trade‑off quantification: estimate true‑positive detection rates on task banks with non‑negligible baseline faults and quantify verifier false‑positive blocking costs. The archived artifacts provide a reproducible template to design such targeted, powered follow‑on experiments.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation (c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) under shared_initial_candidate semantics to test whether a canonical deterministic verifier reduces the proportion of LLM‑generated configurations that would execute with operational faults. For the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini), verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and synthetic/emulated task bank, baseline executions produced zero emulator faults and the verifier did not change outcomes (paired difference = 0.0; bootstrap 95% CI [0.0,0.0]; exact McNemar p = 1.0). This artifact‑grounded null/ceiling outcome is internally consistent with the preregistered design: when identical generated candidates produce no executed faults a verifier cannot reduce executed faults under the shared_initial_candidate contract. Measuring verifier utility under realistic error regimes requires preregistered contracts that permit independent or multiple generator samples, repair‑enabled flows, adversarial task sets, and multi‑model comparisons. The archived artifacts (responses, task manifests, verifier traces, execution manifest, and analysis logs) provide a reproducible baseline and a template for those follow‑on confirmatory designs and power calculations.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure: This study was executed autonomously after an autonomy lock. Human role and autonomy boundary: a human Research Director selected the broad topic family and approved the immutable initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock; no human manually edited technical manuscript content after the lock. Models and orchestration: initial generation used gpt‑5‑mini, orchestrated via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 served as the canonical verifier; an isolated emulator executed candidate configurations. Preregistration and archive: the study was preregistered (study id c1‑gnr‑vv‑2026‑0001) and the execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the study bundle and summarized by the archived execution manifest. Immutable master‑prompt reference (archived): provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Provider‑call audit: hosted model call count = 72 (recorded in the archived execution manifest). No human manual manuscript editing occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Confirmatory ceiling/null outcome: the baseline generator produced zero emulator faults on the preregistered task set, preventing direct measurement of verifier detection benefit.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the design measures verifier effect on the same generated candidate only and does not assess independent per‑condition generation, multi‑sample generation, or repairs unless explicitly permitted by the contract.
Single‑model scope: experiments used one declared model (gpt‑5‑mini); results do not imply generality across models or versions.
Synthetic/emulated tasks: task corpus and emulator executions differ from production devices and live traffic; external validity to production deployments is limited.
Sampling‑parameter uncertainty: archived model configuration records show temperature = null; null indicates provider‑default sampling semantics and is a residual uncertainty recorded in the archive.

Residual contamination risk: deterministic provenance and exact‑match checks were applied, but private training‑data contamination of the hosted model cannot be fully ruled out and remains residual uncertainty.
